classification.difficultyReason: Identify three favourable marbles among thirteen equally likely selections.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the primes from 1 to 15, recognising that 1 is not prime, then apply the taught complement rule and simplify the probability. This is a direct application with no change of representation.

questions.methodNote: Use the complement rule P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A), demonstrated in Example 5. The six primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13, so the required probability is 1 − 6/15 = 3/5.

questions.methodNote: Use the complement rule P(A^c)=1-P(A), demonstrated in Example 5. The multiples of 7 among 1–30 are 7, 14, 21 and 28, giving 1−4/30=13/15.

questions.methodNote: Example 14 on PDF page 28 treats successive coin tosses as independent, assigns probability one half to each head or tail, and multiplies probabilities along a specified sequence. PDF pages 22 and 25 support independent-event multiplication; page 27 explains multiplication along tree branches.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply probabilities for four independent tosses and use a complementary event for at least one head.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the single-toss probabilities and multiply across three independent tosses. The hardest interpretation is that 'the first two tosses only' requires 6, 6, then not 6; each part otherwise specifies one ordered path using the taught method.

questions.mappingNote: Each part specifies one three-stage path: 6/6/6, not-6/not-6/not-6, odd/odd/odd, even/even/even, 6/6/not-6, or 6/not-6/6. The directly assessed method is multiplication of independent probabilities; the conditional-probability material on pages 15–16 is not needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 teaches multiplication of independent-event probabilities. Page 25 explains unchanged stage probabilities with replacement. Page 27 multiplies probabilities along successive branches. Example 14 on page 28 applies fixed independent probabilities to three tosses and multiplies along each required ordered path.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the single-toss probabilities and multiply across three independent tosses. The hardest interpretation is that 'the first two tosses only' requires 6, 6, then not 6; each part otherwise specifies one ordered path using the taught method.

classification.difficultyReason: Read counts from the two-way table and choose the appropriate sample space: all items for part a, but only chocolates for part b. Both probabilities directly apply the taught table method, with routine totals and fraction simplification.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses all table entries as the sample space; part b uses only the chocolate row, matching the taught conditional-table method.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 restricts the sample space to the given event. Page 16 Example 9 uses two-way-table counts for ordinary and conditional probabilities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read counts from the two-way table and choose the appropriate sample space: all items for part a, but only chocolates for part b. Both probabilities directly apply the taught table method, with routine totals and fraction simplification.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguishes replacement from non-replacement, adds probabilities for either order, and uses a complement.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses fixed draw probabilities; part b updates the second draw to four remaining marbles. The mixed-colour events require both orders. The most advanced directly assessed skill is dependent-event probability.
questions.methodNote: Pages 25–27 distinguish replacement and non-replacement, multiply successive draw probabilities, and add disjoint colour orders. Pages 2–3 establish favourable outcomes and total probability 1; page 21 gives independent multiplication; page 28 demonstrates adding branch products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguishes replacement from non-replacement, adds probabilities for either order, and uses a complement.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses replacement to identify independent draws, distinguishes either order from a specified order, and combines the two mutually exclusive parity orders.

questions.mappingNote: Part a counts matching ordered pairs; part b adds the even–odd and odd–even independent paths; part c multiplies probabilities in the specified order. These directly assess independent multistage probability.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 calculate event probabilities by counting equally likely ordered outcomes. Page 21 states the independent-event multiplication rule. Page 25 explains that replacement leaves successive draws independent. Pages 27–28 multiply successive branch probabilities and add probabilities of distinct favourable paths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses replacement to identify independent draws, distinguishes either order from a specified order, and combines the two mutually exclusive parity orders.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied outcome table to count favourable pairs, identify an intersection and apply the taught independence test; the parts scaffold this routine sequence.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied 4×6 sum array must be completed and its 24 equally likely positions counted. Part d directly assesses the page-21 independence criterion, making independence-test the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 distinguish equally likely die pairs from unequal sum outcomes and calculate event probabilities by counting pairs. Page 21 teaches the independence test P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Pages 25–26 reinforce outcome arrays and product comparisons; pages 27–28 show equivalent multistage tree/counting methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied outcome table to count favourable pairs, identify an intersection and apply the taught independence test; the parts scaffold this routine sequence.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly apply the taught restricted-sample-space method: select the 60 mathematics students as the denominator and the 20 studying both as the numerator.

questions.mappingNote: Selecting a mathematics student makes mathematics the conditioning event; physics is the requested event.
questions.methodNote: Restrict the sample space to the conditioning event, then divide the intersection count by the restricted total, as in Example 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly apply the taught restricted-sample-space method: select the 60 mathematics students as the denominator and the 20 studying both as the numerator.

classification.difficultyReason: Count favourable ordered pairs from two selections with repetition.

questions.mappingNote: The two odd-digit selections correspond to the ordered two-dice outcomes in Example 1; repetition is explicitly permitted.
questions.methodNote: List equally likely ordered outcomes, identify the favourable event and divide its size by the sample-space size.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count favourable ordered pairs from two selections with repetition.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the total of 20 marbles and translate red or black, not white, and neither black nor white into favourable colour counts; these require routine linked event interpretations.

questions.mappingNote: The three parts respectively assess a disjoint union, the complement of white and the remaining red category.
questions.methodNote: Use favourable outcomes over total outcomes, add probabilities for mutually exclusive events and use the complement rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the total of 20 marbles and translate red or black, not white, and neither black nor white into favourable colour counts; these require routine linked event interpretations.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the four qualifying ordered colour sequences, multiply their cube-specific probabilities and add them; this links routine taught procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Example 14 supplies the three-stage sequence method; Example 12 supplies multiplication for independent events. The cubes require different branch probabilities.
questions.methodNote: Multiply probabilities along independent successive outcomes and add probabilities of the required mutually exclusive colour sequences.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the four qualifying ordered colour sequences, multiply their cube-specific probabilities and add them; this links routine taught procedures.

classification.difficultyReason: Count multiples in a finite sample space, identify their intersection, and subtract common outcomes for exclusive conditions.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed compound conditions are intersection and exclusion of divisibility events. Conditional probability, independence and multistage experiments are not required.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 establish favourable outcomes and probabilities in a sample space. Pages 8–9 explain complements and intersections. Count multiples among the 100 equally likely integers, then remove the intersection for 'but not' conditions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count multiples in a finite sample space, identify their intersection, and subtract common outcomes for exclusive conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest demand is splitting restricted team selections into disjoint cases; pairing and independent-match probabilities use routine procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Restricted team selection is the most advanced assessed skill; part c additionally assesses independent events.
questions.methodNote: Pages 22 and 28 support multiplying independent probabilities and adding disjoint outcome sequences. Original teaching for unordered team selections and mixed-doubles pairing is absent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The hardest demand is splitting restricted team selections into disjoint cases; pairing and independent-match probabilities use routine procedures.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must construct a joint event by subtraction and distinguish two conditional sample spaces when sampling without replacement.

questions.mappingNote: Parts b and c explicitly restrict the sample space, making conditional probability the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Use complements, conditional probability and successive probabilities without replacement, as taught in the complement section, conditional-probability formula and Example 15.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Students must construct a joint event by subtraction and distinguish two conditional sample spaces when sampling without replacement.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest part requires independently splitting repeated-digit numbers into the disjoint patterns 2+1+1 and 2+2, then choosing digits and counting arrangements without double-counting. The other parts use routine position counting and a complement probability.

questions.mappingNote: The multiplicity cases in a iii are the most advanced directly assessed counting skill; b applies a complement to the set in a i.
questions.methodNote: The chapter supports complements and equally likely multistage outcomes. Original teaching for ordered digit selections and repeated-digit case counting is absent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The hardest part requires independently splitting repeated-digit numbers into the disjoint patterns 2+1+1 and 2+2, then choosing digits and counting arrangements without double-counting. The other parts use routine position counting and a complement probability.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must replace equally likely boxes with equally likely drawer outcomes and condition on the observed diamond.

questions.mappingNote: The diamond observation is a condition that changes the relative likelihood of the possible boxes.
questions.methodNote: List equally likely elementary outcomes and restrict the sample space using the observed event, following the conditional-probability teaching.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Students must replace equally likely boxes with equally likely drawer outcomes and condition on the observed diamond.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses an algebraic complement calculation for two tickets among distinct prize-winning tickets.

questions.mappingNote: The requested at-least-one probability is obtained most directly by complementing the two-ticket losing event.
questions.methodNote: Use the complement rule and successive probabilities without replacement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses an algebraic complement calculation for two tickets among distinct prize-winning tickets.

classification.difficultyReason: Proves a conditional-probability identity using a set intersection and mutual exclusivity.

questions.mappingNote: The proposition directly assesses symbolic conditional probability.
questions.methodNote: Combine the addition rule for mutually exclusive events with the conditional-probability formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves a conditional-probability identity using a set intersection and mutual exclusivity.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must translate grid journeys into arrangements of six right and four upward moves, then recognise that paths through D split into two independently counted segments. Multiplying those segment counts and comparing with the total requires a non-trivial connection between combinatorial counting and equally likely outcomes; part (a) supplies the denominator for part (b).

questions.mappingNote: The probability requires combinatorial counts for both the full path set and paths constrained to pass through D.
questions.methodNote: The chapter supports favourable outcomes divided by equally likely outcomes. Original teaching for monotone lattice-path counting and paths through a vertex is absent.

Multiplying those segment counts and comparing with the total requires a non-trivial connection between combinatorial counting and equally likely outcomes; part (a) supplies the denominator for part (b).
